title: The Iliad
author: Homer
openingText: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled from the day on which the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles, first fell out with one another. And which of the gods was it that set them on to quarrel? It was the son of Jove and Leto; for he was angry with the king and sent a pestilence upon the host to plague the people, because the son of Atreus had dishonoured Chryses his priest.
about:
The Iliad is the Greek epic of the Trojan War — but only of one slice of it, the wrath of Achilles in the war's last year. Achilles, the greatest fighter in the Greek army, is dishonored by his commander Agamemnon and withdraws from battle. Without him the Greeks suffer, his closest friend Patroclus is killed, and Achilles returns to the field to take revenge. The poem ends with the burial of Hector, the Trojan prince Achilles has killed.

Composed orally in Greek around the 8th century BCE and attributed to Homer, the Iliad is the oldest work of Western literature and the foundation of everything that came after. It is roughly 15,000 lines of dactylic hexameter. It is also one of the great poems of grief — the second half is mostly about the death of Patroclus and what death does to those who survive.

angleCards.title: The wrath of Achilles.
angleCards.text: The poem announces its subject in the first word: rage. Everything that happens — the deaths, the reversals, the grief — flows from one man's wounded pride. What does Homer want you to think about that?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the wrath of Achilles from the opening quarrel to its final exhaustion — and understand what Homer is saying about pride, honor, and the destruction they bring.

angleCards.title: Hector, not Achilles.
angleCards.text: Achilles is the hero. Hector is the one you root for. He fights not for glory but for his city, his wife, his son. Homer makes the Trojan side fully human — that is the poem's moral achievement.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Iliad through Hector's eyes — the man defending something real — and understand why Homer makes the losing side so much more sympathetic.

angleCards.title: The gods as meddling personalities.
angleCards.text: Zeus, Athena, Apollo, Aphrodite — they quarrel on Olympus while men die below. They play favorites, change outcomes, rescue their favorites from death. Homer's gods are not wise or just. They are powerful and petty.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the divine interference throughout the poem — who the gods favor, why, and what Homer reveals about fate, free will, and the relationship between humans and the divine.

angleCards.title: Honor and its cost.
angleCards.text: Every warrior in the Iliad is obsessed with kleos — glory, reputation, being remembered. It drives every decision. But Homer keeps showing you what the pursuit of honor destroys: armies, friendships, families, lives.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the logic of honor (kleos) through the poem — what drives these men, what it costs them, and whether Homer endorses or questions the heroic code he is depicting.

cast.name: Achilles
cast.description: Son of Peleus and the goddess Thetis. Knows he will die young at Troy, and chose it over a long, forgotten life. His rage at Agamemnon sets the entire poem in motion.

cast.name: Hector
cast.description: Eldest son of Priam, husband of Andromache, father of an infant son. The Trojans' greatest defender — and the man the poem makes you love most.

cast.name: Agamemnon
cast.description: Commander of all the Greek forces. Powerful, proud, and politically clumsy. His arrogance in Book I triggers everything that follows.

cast.name: Patroclus
cast.description: Achilles's closest friend, present at the ships throughout the early books. His fate is the pivot on which the second half of the poem turns.

cast.name: Priam
cast.description: The aged king who watches from the walls as the war takes his sons. His courage and grief give the poem its most devastating moment.

cast.name: Helen
cast.description: The most beautiful woman in the world, whose abduction from Sparta by Paris brought a thousand ships to Troy. She appears rarely but always with a weight of guilt Homer lets her feel.

acclaim.quote: The true hero, the true subject, the center of the Iliad is force.
acclaim.context: The Iliad, or the Poem of Force, 1939

whyItMatters.title: Where the West Begins
whyItMatters.body: The Iliad is the oldest work of Western literature and the soil everything else grew from. Homer's Achilles, his Hector, his Priam are characters that Plato, Virgil, Dante, Milton, and Joyce all wrote in conversation with. To read the Iliad is to start at the source.

whyItMatters.title: Force as the Center
whyItMatters.body: Simone Weil read the Iliad as the great poem of force — what violence does to the people who use it and the people who suffer it. The poem does not glorify war. It shows fighters becoming things, and it shows what is left of them when the fighting stops.

whyItMatters.title: The Loss of Patroclus
whyItMatters.body: The second half of the poem is mostly grief. Achilles loses Patroclus and the rest of the poem is about that loss — refusing to eat, refusing to bury him, finally meeting Priam who has lost his own son to the same fight. The poem argues that war does not win against grief.
